sections.title: Name and taxonomic concept
sections.text: The name used here is Russula maculata Quél. (1878), in the Russulaceae; some sources cite the authority as Quél. & Roze. Species Fungorum records several historical combinations and synonyms, including Russulina maculata and Russula veternosa var. maculata. A molecular study anchored to the epitype supports the concept of R. maculata, while showing that spotted russulas traditionally grouped under that name also include distinct species, including R. nympharum. The spots therefore characterize a group and are not enough to identify the species; microscopic characters matter.

sections.title: Cap and spots
sections.text: The fruitbody is firm and fleshy; the cap reaches about 4–10 cm across, hemispherical at first, then expanded and sometimes shallowly depressed at the centre. Its smooth, shiny cuticle varies from pinkish cream or orange to red, often paler at the centre and fading with age. Small yellow-brown, ochre or rusty spots appear on the cap and become more conspicuous with age; these are natural stains associated with browning of the flesh, not merely stuck-on debris.

sections.title: Gills, stem and flesh
sections.text: The gills are crowded and brittle, cream at first then yellowish; they may fork and connect near the stem, and develop yellow-brown or rusty spots with age. The stem is cylindrical to slightly clavate, white and sometimes pink-flushed, firm when young then spongy; it yellows or browns with age or handling, especially near the base. The firm white flesh also develops yellow-brown discoloration after injury or with age. The odour is described as fruity or cedar-like; the taste is acrid, especially in the gills. The spore print is yellow.

sections.title: Habitat and caution
sections.text: It grows on the ground in temperate broadleaf woodland; studied collections were associated with oaks, beech, hornbeam and lime. Regional accounts report it especially in open woodland, often on calcareous soils, from summer into early autumn; these periods are not universal. It can be confused with other red or spotted russulas, including R. nympharum, which molecular and microscopic study separated despite a very similar field appearance. It is considered inedible because of its acrid taste; this does not mean this entry establishes toxicity. Do not eat a russula identified from a photograph.

traits: Firm, fleshy brittlegill with a cap about 4–10 cm across, convex then expanded and sometimes depressed at the centre
Cap pinkish cream, orange or red, often fading; marked with small yellow-brown, ochre or rusty macules
Crowded, brittle gills, cream then yellowish, sometimes forked near the stem and developing rusty spots with age
White, sometimes pink-flushed stem, firm when young then spongy, yellowing or browning with age and handling
Firm white flesh develops yellow-brown stains after injury; fruity or cedar-like odour, acrid taste; yellow spore print
On the ground in broadleaf woodland, associated notably with oak, beech, hornbeam or lime
safetyNote: Russula maculata is considered inedible because of its acrid taste; this entry does not classify it as toxic. Spots and cap colour are not enough for secure identification, and very similar russulas may require microscopic examination. Do not eat a specimen based on a photo or this entry.
